newsitem.title: CHINA: HK a delicate mission for China military star.
newsitem.headline: HK a delicate mission for China military star.

text.p: China's post-colonial Hong Kong garrison commander, Major-General Liu Zhenwu, is a man with a delicate mission -- but star-struck British officers seem to think he can pull it off.

Liu must lead China's military in a territory where faith in the People's Liberation Army was shattered in 1989 when troops and tanks crushed pro-democracy demonstrations centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square, killing hundreds.

In conversations with officers of the British army, which will make a final withdrawal from Hong Kong after the handover of sovereignty at midnight on June 30, Liu has signalled his desire to buff up the PLA's tarnished image.
His British counterparts appear to believe that Liu, a 53-year-old career soldier, is the right man for the job.

Liu will have his work cut out after China announced just four days before the July 1 Hong Kong handover that 4,000 troops backed by armoured personnel carriers would enter the territory at around dawn on the first day of Chinese sovereignty.
One Hong Kong-based officer described Liu as "a very experienced, sensible and pleasant gentleman" after a two-trip charm offensive by the future garrison commander last year.
A former tutor at a British defence college where Liu studied for a year in the late 1980s was even more effusive.

"His personality combines intelligence and humour and the ability to get on with people," gushed tutor Major General John Evans earlier this year. "At the end of the year he quite genuinely had our respect and affection."
Liu even has the right given name for the job: the Chinese character "Zhen" can be read as "garrison", while "Wu" means "military".

Liu was born in China's southern Hunan province in 1944, when much of the nation was under occupation by Japanese imperial forces. He was just a child when the Communist Party won its civil war against the Nationalists in 1949.
Liu joined the army at 17 and spent his military career in a number of posts in the Guangzhou Military Region, which covers five southern provinces, newspapers in Hong Kong have reported.
Chinese Defence Ministry officials were unwilling to give details of Liu's career -- or even to confirm his birthday.

He is said to be a moderniser in an army that revised its Maoist "People's War" tactics only in the 1980s, and is also considered a strict disciplinarian -- a trait that could help ensure his troops do not antagonise the local population.

Liu has officially served as commander of the military force of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region since October 1994, but, in an apparent nod to Hong Kong sensibilities, the formation of the unit was not formally announced until 1996.
For many residents in Hong Kong, the strongest impression of the PLA remains the televised sight of tanks and soldiers seizing control of Beijing's avenues from students in 1989.
A dispute between one senior officer and Hong Kong border officials this month raised hackles in the territory, where PLA privileges are seen as a potential threat to the rule of law.
China has rushed to assure doubters that it is sending only its finest troops to Hong Kong and that they will be barred from the business dealings that are a hallmark of PLA life in China.

The post-colonial garrison will even have its own pig farm to make it more self-sufficient -- an important point for soldiers who will be paid wages considered a pittance in the booming mercantile city they will defend.
For all Liu's qualifications, the Major-General's official income would seem to leave him little chance to partake of the social high life enjoyed by some of his British predecessors.
Liu will earn only 1,200 yuan ($145) a month, official Chinese media have reported. The Hong Kong government-set minimum wage for a domestic servant is about $500 a month.
